claim: Monocyte counts are increased during human tuberculosis (TB).
source: Monocyte counts are increased during human tuberculosis (TB) but it has not been determined whether Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) directly regulates myeloid commitment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact, supported by citations in the introduction (Rogers, 1928; Schmitt et al., 1977; Berry et al., 2010; Zak et al., 2016).

claim: Exposure to Mtb directs primary human CD34+ cells to differentiate into monocytes/macrophages.
source: We demonstrated that exposure to Mtb directs primary human CD34+ cells to differentiate into monocytes/macrophages.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In vitro myeloid conversion did not require type I or type II IFN signaling.
source: In vitro myeloid conversion did not require type I or type II IFN signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using neutralizing antibodies shown in Figure 4d,e.

claim: Mtb enhanced IL-6 responses by CD34+ cell cultures.
source: In contrast, Mtb enhanced IL-6 responses by CD34+ cell cultures and IL-6R neutralization inhibited myeloid differentiation and decreased mycobacterial growth in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 including RNA-seq, qPCR, and flow cytometry.

claim: IL-6R neutralization inhibited myeloid differentiation and decreased mycobacterial growth in vitro.
source: In contrast, Mtb enhanced IL-6 responses by CD34+ cell cultures and IL-6R neutralization inhibited myeloid differentiation and decreased mycobacterial growth in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f-i using anti-IL-6R antibody.

claim: A myeloid IL-6/IL6R/CEBP gene module is associated with disease severity in TB patients.
source: Integrated systems biology analysis of transcriptomic, proteomic and genomic data of large data sets of healthy controls and TB patients established the existence of a myeloid IL-6/IL6R/CEBP gene module associated with disease severity.
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of multiple published datasets shown in Figure 5.

claim: The IL6/IL6R/CEBP gene module has undergone recent evolutionary selection, including Neanderthal introgression.
source: Furthermore, genetic and functional analysis revealed the IL6/IL6R/CEBP gene module has undergone recent evolutionary selection, including Neanderthal introgression and human pathogen adaptation, connected to systemic monocyte counts.
evidence: This is supported by evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 6, including Neanderthal introgression data.

claim: The IL6/IL6R/CEBP gene module is connected to systemic monocyte counts.
source: Furthermore, genetic and functional analysis revealed the IL6/IL6R/CEBP gene module has undergone recent evolutionary selection, including Neanderthal introgression and human pathogen adaptation, connected to systemic monocyte counts.
evidence: This is supported by GWAS data and correlation analysis shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Mtb co-opts an evolutionary recent IFN-IL6-CEBP feed-forward loop, increasing myeloid differentiation linked to severe TB in humans.
source: These results suggest Mtb co-opts an evolutionary recent IFN-IL6-CEBP feed-forward loop, increasing myeloid differentiation linked to severe TB in humans.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating multiple lines of evidence from in vitro experiments, systems biology analysis, and evolutionary genetics.

claim: Mtb H37Rv was associated with CD34+ cells following 4 hr exposure to mycobacteria.
source: First, by using a fluorescent dye (syto-24) which does not influence bacteria infectivity (data not shown), flow cytometry experiments demonstrated that Mtb were associated with CD34+ cells following 4 hr exposure to mycobacteria (Figure 1a,b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1a,b.

claim: Approximately 69% of CD34+ cells were associated with Mtb at 4 hours post-infection.
source: At that time point, we observed ~69% of CD34+ and ~79% of CD14+ associated with Mtb (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is quantitative data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Approximately 79% of CD14+ cells were associated with Mtb at 4 hours post-infection.
source: At that time point, we observed ~69% of CD34+ and ~79% of CD14+ associated with Mtb (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is quantitative data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The MFI measurements of Mtb association within the CD34+ cell population were approximately 4-fold lower compared to CD14+ cells.
source: When compared to CD14+ cells, which are highly phagocytic cells, the MFI measurements within the CD34+ cell population were found to be ~4 x lower (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is quantitative data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 1d.

claim: PBMC CD34+ cells may be permissive to Mtb infection in vitro.
source: These data suggest that PBMC CD34+ cells may be permissive to Mtb infection in vitro.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the flow cytometry data showing Mtb association with CD34+ cells.

claim: Purified cord blood derived CD34+ cells display comparable % and MFI of Mtb association as those seen in PBMC CD34+ cells.
source: Similarly, purified cord blood derived CD34+ cells display comparable % and MFI as those seen in PBMC CD34+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Human primary Lin-CD34+ cells can be infected by Mtb in vitro and in vivo.
source: These findings raise the possibility that although human primary Lin-CD34+ cells can be infected by Mtb in vitro and in vivo (Tornack et al., 2017), this cell population may display intrinsic resistance to Mtb infection as it has been reported for other bacterial species (Kolb-Mäurer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the current study's in vitro data and a citation to Tornack et al., 2017 for in vivo data.

claim: CD34+ cells may display intrinsic resistance to Mtb infection.
source: These findings raise the possibility that although human primary Lin-CD34+ cells can be infected by Mtb in vitro and in vivo (Tornack et al., 2017), this cell population may display intrinsic resistance to Mtb infection as it has been reported for other bacterial species (Kolb-Mäurer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower MFI in CD34+ cells compared to CD14+ cells, and supported by citation to Kolb-Mäurer et al., 2002.

claim: Mtb H37Rv exhibited approximately 1.5 log growth in purified cord-blood CD34+ cells at 5 days post infection.
source: When sorted purified cord-blood CD34+ cells were exposed to Mtb H37Rv (MOI3) and cultivated in StemSpan SFEM II (Bodine et al., 1991; Keller et al., 1995), bacilli numbers exhibited a ~ 1.5 log growth at 5 days post infection (dpi) (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is quantitative CFU data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Purified CD14+ cells displayed higher bacterial proliferation than purified CD34+ cells over time.
source: As a control, purified CD14+ cells displayed higher bacterial proliferation than purified CD34+ cells over time (Figure 1-Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Mtb infects and replicates in primary human CD34+ cell cultures in vitro.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that Mtb infects and replicates in primary human CD34+ cell cultures in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CFU and microscopy data presented in Figure 1.

claim: At one day post-infection, bacilli were more associated with the surface of round cells.
source: While at one dpi bacilli were more associated with the surface of round cells (Figure 1f), at five dpi intracellular bacteria were associated with cells with abundant cytoplasm (Figure 1f), suggesting that Mtb-exposed cultures displayed increased frequencies of cells exhibiting morphological alterations over time (Figure 1f, right panel).
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1f.

claim: At five days post-infection, intracellular bacteria were associated with cells with abundant cytoplasm.
source: While at one dpi bacilli were more associated with the surface of round cells (Figure 1f), at five dpi intracellular bacteria were associated with cells with abundant cytoplasm (Figure 1f), suggesting that Mtb-exposed cultures displayed increased frequencies of cells exhibiting morphological alterations over time (Figure 1f, right panel).
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Mtb-exposed cultures displayed increased frequencies of cells exhibiting morphological alterations over time.
source: While at one dpi bacilli were more associated with the surface of round cells (Figure 1f), at five dpi intracellular bacteria were associated with cells with abundant cytoplasm (Figure 1f), suggesting that Mtb-exposed cultures displayed increased frequencies of cells exhibiting morphological alterations over time (Figure 1f, right panel).
evidence: This is based on quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 1f, right panel.

claim: Giemsa staining presented higher frequency of cytoplasm-richer cells in bacteria-exposed vs uninfected cell cultures.
source: Indeed, Giemsa staining (Figure 1g, arrows) presented higher frequency of cytoplasm- richer cells in bacteria-exposed vs uninfected cell cultures (Figure 1g, right panel), thus suggesting that Mtb infection enhances cellular differentiation by CD34+ cells in vitro.
evidence: This is based on Giemsa staining and quantification shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Mtb infection enhances cellular differentiation by CD34+ cells in vitro.
source: Indeed, Giemsa staining (Figure 1g, arrows) presented higher frequency of cytoplasm- richer cells in bacteria-exposed vs uninfected cell cultures (Figure 1g, right panel), thus suggesting that Mtb infection enhances cellular differentiation by CD34+ cells in vitro.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the morphological changes observed in Giemsa staining.

claim: Mtb infection increased the expression of lineage-specific regulators of myeloid differentiation (SPI1, CEBPB, CEBPA, EGR2 and STAT2).
source: Interestingly, Mtb infection increased the expression of lineage-specific regulators of myeloid (GRAN/MONO) (SPI1, CEBPB, CEBPA, EGR2 and STAT2), but not lymphoid (B and T CELL) (GABPA, SOX5, TCF3, GATA3, LEF1, RORA and LMO7) or megakaryoid/erythroid (EARLY/LATE ERY) (GATA1, FOXO3, NFE2, TAL1) differentiation (Figure 2a – Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of transcription factors shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Mtb infection did not increase the expression of lineage-specific regulators of lymphoid differentiation (GABPA, SOX5, TCF3, GATA3, LEF1, RORA and LMO7).
source: Interestingly, Mtb infection increased the expression of lineage-specific regulators of myeloid (GRAN/MONO) (SPI1, CEBPB, CEBPA, EGR2 and STAT2), but not lymphoid (B and T CELL) (GABPA, SOX5, TCF3, GATA3, LEF1, RORA and LMO7) or megakaryoid/erythroid (EARLY/LATE ERY) (GATA1, FOXO3, NFE2, TAL1) differentiation (Figure 2a – Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of transcription factors shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Mtb infection did not increase the expression of lineage-specific regulators of megakaryoid/erythroid differentiation (GATA1, FOXO3, NFE2, TAL1).
source: Interestingly, Mtb infection increased the expression of lineage-specific regulators of myeloid (GRAN/MONO) (SPI1, CEBPB, CEBPA, EGR2 and STAT2), but not lymphoid (B and T CELL) (GABPA, SOX5, TCF3, GATA3, LEF1, RORA and LMO7) or megakaryoid/erythroid (EARLY/LATE ERY) (GATA1, FOXO3, NFE2, TAL1) differentiation (Figure 2a – Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of transcription factors shown in Figure 2a.

claim: CellRouter signature score of the GRAN/MONO gene set was found to be increased in Mtb vs uninfected samples in all time points studied.
source: Similarly, CellRouter (Lummertz da Rocha et al., 2018) signature score of the GRAN/MONO gene set was found to be increased in Mtb vs uninfected samples in all time points studied (Figure 2b - Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on CellRouter analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: mRNA samples from Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells presented enrichment of monocyte/macrophage profiles.
source: Figure 2c (Figure 2—source data 1) shows that mRNA samples from Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells presented enrichment of monocyte/macrophage profiles, but not other mature cell populations such as lymphocytes or dendritic cells.
evidence: This is based on CellNet analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: mRNA samples from Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells did not present enrichment of lymphocyte or dendritic cell profiles.
source: Figure 2c (Figure 2—source data 1) shows that mRNA samples from Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells presented enrichment of monocyte/macrophage profiles, but not other mature cell populations such as lymphocytes or dendritic cells.
evidence: This is based on CellNet analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: At five days post-infection, CD34+ cell cultures displayed increased frequencies of cells positive for CD11b.
source: Additionally, at five dpi, CD34+ cell cultures displayed increased frequencies of cells positive for CD11b (Figure 2d), a surface molecule expressed during myeloid differentiation (Hickstein et al., 1989; Rosmarin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: CD11b is a surface molecule expressed during myeloid differentiation.
source: Additionally, at five dpi, CD34+ cell cultures displayed increased frequencies of cells positive for CD11b (Figure 2d), a surface molecule expressed during myeloid differentiation (Hickstein et al., 1989; Rosmarin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Hickstein et al., 1989 and Rosmarin et al., 1989.

claim: Mtb drives human primary CD34+ cells towards myeloid differentiation.
source: Together, these data suggest that Mtb drives human primary CD34+ cells towards myeloid differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcriptomic and flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Mtb enhanced the frequency of CD64+CD4+CD34+ cells at five days post-infection.
source: Corroborating our hypothesis, Mtb enhanced the frequency of CD64+CD4+CD34+ cells (Figure 2e–h) at five dpi, but not CD10+CD34+ (lymphoid) or CD41a+CD34+ (megakaryoid) progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2e-h.

claim: Mtb did not enhance the frequency of CD10+CD34+ (lymphoid) or CD41a+CD34+ (megakaryoid) progenitors.
source: Corroborating our hypothesis, Mtb enhanced the frequency of CD64+CD4+CD34+ cells (Figure 2e–h) at five dpi, but not CD10+CD34+ (lymphoid) or CD41a+CD34+ (megakaryoid) progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Lin-CD34+ cells from PBMC samples from healthy donors exposed to Mtb displayed increased frequency of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells.
source: Similarly, Lin-CD34+ cells from PBMC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) samples from healthy donors exposed to Mtb displayed increased frequency of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells and augmented levels of CD38 and HLA-DR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c), two molecules associated with advanced stage of cellular differentiation (Cimato et al., 2016; De Bruyn et al., 1995; Terstappen et al., 1991).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Mtb-exposed Lin-CD34+ cells from PBMC displayed augmented levels of CD38 and HLA-DR.
source: Similarly, Lin-CD34+ cells from PBMC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) samples from healthy donors exposed to Mtb displayed increased frequency of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells and augmented levels of CD38 and HLA-DR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c), two molecules associated with advanced stage of cellular differentiation (Cimato et al., 2016; De Bruyn et al., 1995; Terstappen et al., 1991).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: CD38 and HLA-DR are molecules associated with advanced stage of cellular differentiation.
source: Similarly, Lin-CD34+ cells from PBMC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) samples from healthy donors exposed to Mtb displayed increased frequency of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells and augmented levels of CD38 and HLA-DR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c), two molecules associated with advanced stage of cellular differentiation (Cimato et al., 2016; De Bruyn et al., 1995; Terstappen et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Cimato et al., 2016; De Bruyn et al., 1995; Terstappen et al., 1991.

claim: Mtb-exposed bulk bone marrow samples from two healthy individuals showed an increased % CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells compared to baseline levels.
source: When compared to their base line levels, we also observed an increased % CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells in Mtb-exposed bulk bone marrow samples from two healthy individuals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, p=0.08).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data from bone marrow samples shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Frequencies of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells were higher in cultures infected with live H37Rv Mtb than those exposed to heat-killed bacteria.
source: In addition, frequencies of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells were higher in cultures infected to live H37Rv Mtb than those exposed to heat-killed (HK) bacteria (Figure 2f,g).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data comparing live and heat-killed Mtb shown in Figure 2f,g.

claim: The observed cellular phenotype was mostly due to the activities of live pathogen and only partially to mycobacterial PAMPs.
source: These results suggest that the observed cellular phenotype was mostly due to the activities of live pathogen and only partially to mycobacterial PAMPs such as TLR2 (Ara-LAM) or TLR9 (Mtb gDNA) agonists (Bafica et al., 2005; Underhill et al., 1999), which induced CD38 and HLA-DR, but not CD4 and CD64 expression in CD34+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing live vs heat-killed Mtb and PAMP stimulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: TLR2 (Ara-LAM) or TLR9 (Mtb gDNA) agonists induced CD38 and HLA-DR, but not CD4 and CD64 expression in CD34+ cells.
source: These results suggest that the observed cellular phenotype was mostly due to the activities of live pathogen and only partially to mycobacterial PAMPs such as TLR2 (Ara-LAM) or TLR9 (Mtb gDNA) agonists (Bafica et al., 2005; Underhill et al., 1999), which induced CD38 and HLA-DR, but not CD4 and CD64 expression in CD34+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data with PAMP stimulation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Increased frequency of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells was observed when cell cultures were exposed to a clinical isolate of Mtb.
source: Importantly, increased frequency of CD4+CD64+CD34+ cells was also observed when cell cultures were exposed to a clinical isolate of Mtb (Figure 2h), ruling out a possible genetic factor associated with the laboratory strain H37Rv (Brites and Gagneux, 2015).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data with clinical isolate shown in Figure 2h.

claim: CD34+ cell death was not enhanced by Mtb infection.
source: Furthermore, CD34+ cell death was not enhanced by Mtb infection as demonstrated by the use of a live-and-dead probe and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) quantification in cell culture supernatants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: This is based on viability staining and LDH assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: Live Mtb directs primary human CD34+ cells towards myeloid differentiation in vitro.
source: Together, these data indicate live Mtb directs primary human CD34+ cells towards myeloid differentiation in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the flow cytometry and transcriptomic data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Live H37Rv or clinical isolate Mtb enhanced expression of the monocyte surface molecule CD14.
source: Live H37Rv (Figure 3a,e) or clinical isolate Mtb, (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) but not Leishmania infantum promastigotes (data not shown), enhanced expression of the monocyte surface molecule CD14, confirming the observed monocyte/macrophage output enrichment by CellNet analysis (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3a,e and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Leishmania infantum promastigotes did not enhance expression of the monocyte surface molecule CD14.
source: Live H37Rv (Figure 3a,e) or clinical isolate Mtb, (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) but not Leishmania infantum promastigotes (data not shown), enhanced expression of the monocyte surface molecule CD14, confirming the observed monocyte/macrophage output enrichment by CellNet analysis (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: CD14+ cells started to emerge at low levels at day three in both uninfected and Mtb-exposed cell cultures.
source: Interestingly, in this in vitro culture system, CD14+ cells started to emerge at low levels at day three in both uninfected and Mtb-exposed cell cultures, while enhancement in monocyte frequency was observed in Mtb-stimulated cells at later time points, that is at 7 and 10 dpi. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on time course flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Enhancement in monocyte frequency was observed in Mtb-stimulated cells at 7 and 10 days post-infection.
source: Interestingly, in this in vitro culture system, CD14+ cells started to emerge at low levels at day three in both uninfected and Mtb-exposed cell cultures, while enhancement in monocyte frequency was observed in Mtb-stimulated cells at later time points, that is at 7 and 10 dpi. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on time course flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CD14+ cells induced by Mtb displayed similar MFI expression of CD11b, HLA-DR, CD64 and CD16 surface molecules compared to control cell cultures.
source: Compared to control cell cultures, CD14+ cells induced by Mtb displayed similar MFI expression of CD11b, HLA-DR, CD64 and CD16 surface molecules (Figure 3i) and most, but not all experiments presented increased frequency of CD14+CD16+ monocytes (Figure 3j), which were previously associated with severe pulmonary TB (Balboa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Most, but not all experiments presented increased frequency of CD14+CD16+ monocytes in Mtb-exposed cultures.
source: Compared to control cell cultures, CD14+ cells induced by Mtb displayed similar MFI expression of CD11b, HLA-DR, CD64 and CD16 surface molecules (Figure 3i) and most, but not all experiments presented increased frequency of CD14+CD16+ monocytes (Figure 3j), which were previously associated with severe pulmonary TB (Balboa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: CD14+CD16+ monocytes were previously associated with severe pulmonary TB.
source: Compared to control cell cultures, CD14+ cells induced by Mtb displayed similar MFI expression of CD11b, HLA-DR, CD64 and CD16 surface molecules (Figure 3i) and most, but not all experiments presented increased frequency of CD14+CD16+ monocytes (Figure 3j), which were previously associated with severe pulmonary TB (Balboa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Balboa et al., 2011.

claim: Mtb enhanced the frequency of CD16+CD66b+ neutrophils in the majority but not all samples tested.
source: Moreover, albeit not statistically significant, Mtb enhanced the frequency of CD16+CD66b+ neutrophils in the majority but not all samples tested (Figure 3b,f).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b,f.

claim: HK Mtb did not stimulate monocyte or neutrophil output.
source: In contrast, HK Mtb did not stimulate monocyte or neutrophil output (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data comparing live and heat-killed Mtb shown in Figure 3e,f.

claim: Megakaryoid/platelet-, dendritic cell-, or erythroid-associated markers were unchanged after exposure to live or HK Mtb.
source: As expected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), megakaryoid/platelet- (Figure 3c,g), dendritic cell- (Figure 3d,h) or erythroid- (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) associated markers were unchanged after exposure to live or HK Mtb.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c,d,g,h and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Mtb selectively favors the generation of monocytes and, to a lesser extent, neutrophils, by human CD34+ cells in vitro.
source: Altogether, these results suggest Mtb selectively favors the generation of monocytes and, to a lesser extent, neutrophils, by human CD34+ cells in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Reactome pathway analysis of genes differentially expressed between Mtb-infected versus uninfected conditions displayed enrichment of 'cytokine signaling in immune system'.
source: Cytokines are important triggers of Lin-CD34+ differentiation in vivo and in vitro (Endele et al., 2014; Hoggatt et al., 2016; Zhang and Lodish, 2008) and Reactome pathway analysis of genes differentially expressed between Mtb-infected versus uninfected conditions displayed enrichment of 'cytokine signaling in immune system' (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d; n = 3 donors, two independent experiments - Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on Reactome pathway analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: A significant enrichment of IL6 was observed in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells.
source: Among several genes, we observed a significant enrichment of IL6 (Supplementary file 1 - Figure 2—source data 1), a key HSPC-derived regulator of myeloid differentiation in mouse and human models (Jansen et al., 1992; Zhao et al., 2014) which was confirmed in our system by the addition of exogenous IL-6 to CD34+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data and confirmed by exogenous IL-6 addition shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: IL-6 is a key HSPC-derived regulator of myeloid differentiation in mouse and human models.
source: Among several genes, we observed a significant enrichment of IL6 (Supplementary file 1 - Figure 2—source data 1), a key HSPC-derived regulator of myeloid differentiation in mouse and human models (Jansen et al., 1992; Zhao et al., 2014) which was confirmed in our system by the addition of exogenous IL-6 to CD34+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Jansen et al., 1992 and Zhao et al., 2014.

claim: Cytokine receptors, including IL6R, as well as their cytokine partners, containing IL6, were enriched in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cell cultures.
source: Moreover, cytokine receptors, including IL6R, as well as their cytokine partners, containing IL6, were enriched in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cell cultures (Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b - Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Increased IL6 expression was confirmed by qPCR.
source: Similarly, increased IL6 expression was confirmed by qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: 'Interferon signaling' and 'interferon alpha/beta' pathways were significantly enriched in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells.
source: In addition, 'interferon signaling' and 'interferon alpha/beta' pathways were significantly enriched in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d and Supplementary file 1 - Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Five donors displayed increased levels of IFNA2, IFNB and IFNG transcripts in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells, albeit at a lower level relative to IL6 mRNA.
source: This was confirmed in five donors, which displayed increased levels of IFNA2, IFNB and IFNG transcripts, albeit at a lower level relative to IL6 mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as MX1, ISG15 and IFI16 were enhanced in Mtb-stimulated CD34+ cells from five different donors.
source: Importantly, interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as MX1, ISG15 and IFI16 as well as IL-6R-stimulated genes such as IL1RA, GRB2 and CXCL8 were enhanced in Mtb-stimulated CD34+ cells from five different donors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), suggesting IL-6 and IFN signaling are active in these cells.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: IL-6R-stimulated genes such as IL1RA, GRB2 and CXCL8 were enhanced in Mtb-stimulated CD34+ cells from five different donors.
source: Importantly, interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as MX1, ISG15 and IFI16 as well as IL-6R-stimulated genes such as IL1RA, GRB2 and CXCL8 were enhanced in Mtb-stimulated CD34+ cells from five different donors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), suggesting IL-6 and IFN signaling are active in these cells.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: IL-6 and IFN signaling are active in Mtb-stimulated CD34+ cells.
source: Importantly, interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as MX1, ISG15 and IFI16 as well as IL-6R-stimulated genes such as IL1RA, GRB2 and CXCL8 were enhanced in Mtb-stimulated CD34+ cells from five different donors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), suggesting IL-6 and IFN signaling are active in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of ISGs and IL-6R-stimulated genes.

claim: HSPCs produce IL-6 following microbial stimuli.
source: Corroborating previous findings showing that HSPCs produce IL-6 following microbial stimuli (Allakhverdi and Delespesse, 2012), live Mtb also induced intracellular IL-6 production in Lin-CD34+ cells from bacteria-exposed PBMC 1d cultures (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Allakhverdi and Delespesse, 2012.

claim: Live Mtb induced intracellular IL-6 production in Lin-CD34+ cells from bacteria-exposed PBMC 1d cultures.
source: Corroborating previous findings showing that HSPCs produce IL-6 following microbial stimuli (Allakhverdi and Delespesse, 2012), live Mtb also induced intracellular IL-6 production in Lin-CD34+ cells from bacteria-exposed PBMC 1d cultures (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: 1d culture supernatants of purified CD34+ cells exposed to live Mtb presented augmented levels of IL-6.
source: This was confirmed in 1d culture supernatants of purified CD34+ cells exposed to live Mtb which presented augmented levels of IL-6, but not IFN-γ, IL-1β or TNF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is based on ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: 1d culture supernatants of purified CD34+ cells exposed to live Mtb did not present augmented levels of IFN-γ, IL-1β or TNF.
source: This was confirmed in 1d culture supernatants of purified CD34+ cells exposed to live Mtb which presented augmented levels of IL-6, but not IFN-γ, IL-1β or TNF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is based on ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: HK Mtb stimulated production of IL-6.
source: Interestingly, while HK Mtb also stimulated production of IL-6 (Figure 4c), dead bacteria did not induce CD38, CD4 and CD64 expression in PBMC Lin-CD34+ cells as seen in cell cultures exposed to live Mtb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is based on intracellular flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Dead bacteria did not induce CD38, CD4 and CD64 expression in PBMC Lin-CD34+ cells as seen in cell cultures exposed to live Mtb.
source: Interestingly, while HK Mtb also stimulated production of IL-6 (Figure 4c), dead bacteria did not induce CD38, CD4 and CD64 expression in PBMC Lin-CD34+ cells as seen in cell cultures exposed to live Mtb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claim: qPCR experiments with HK Mtb-exposed purified CD34+ cells did not show induction of ISG STAT1 compared to live pathogen.
source: When compared to the live pathogen, qPCR experiments with HK Mtb-exposed purified CD34+ cells did not show induction of ISG STAT1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g), suggesting the existence of cross talking regulatory pathways between live Mtb, IL-6 and IFN signaling to boost myeloid differentiation in vitro.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g.

claim: There is cross talking of regulatory pathways between live Mtb, IL-6 and IFN signaling to boost myeloid differentiation in vitro.
source: When compared to the live pathogen, qPCR experiments with HK Mtb-exposed purified CD34+ cells did not show induction of ISG STAT1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g), suggesting the existence of cross talking regulatory pathways between live Mtb, IL-6 and IFN signaling to boost myeloid differentiation in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of live vs heat-killed Mtb on ISG and differentiation markers.

claim: Type I IFN signaling was necessary for Mtb-stimulated ISGs such as STAT1 and MX1 transcription.
source: While type I IFN signaling was necessary for Mtb-stimulated ISGs such as STAT1 and MX1 transcription (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h), neither type I nor type II IFN signaling pathways were required for Mtb-enhanced monocyte/granulocyte conversion (Figure 4d,e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data with anti-IFNAR2 treatment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Neither type I nor type II IFN signaling pathways were required for Mtb-enhanced monocyte/granulocyte conversion.
source: While type I IFN signaling was necessary for Mtb-stimulated ISGs such as STAT1 and MX1 transcription (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h), neither type I nor type II IFN signaling pathways were required for Mtb-enhanced monocyte/granulocyte conversion (Figure 4d,e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data with anti-IFNAR2 and anti-IFN-γ treatment shown in Figure 4d,e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Neutralizing anti-IL-6Ra antibody inhibited background levels of CD14+ monocytes and CD66b+ granulocytes.
source: In contrast, neutralizing anti-IL-6Ra antibody (α-IL-6R) inhibited background levels of CD14+ monocytes and CD66b+ granulocytes, as well as Mtb-enhanced myeloid differentiation by CD34+ cell cultures (Figure 4f–h) but not transcription of STAT1 and MX1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data with anti-IL-6R treatment shown in Figure 4f-h.

claim: Neutralizing anti-IL-6Ra antibody inhibited Mtb-enhanced myeloid differentiation by CD34+ cell cultures.
source: In contrast, neutralizing anti-IL-6Ra antibody (α-IL-6R) inhibited background levels of CD14+ monocytes and CD66b+ granulocytes, as well as Mtb-enhanced myeloid differentiation by CD34+ cell cultures (Figure 4f–h) but not transcription of STAT1 and MX1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data with anti-IL-6R treatment shown in Figure 4f-h.

claim: Anti-IL-6R did not inhibit transcription of STAT1 and MX1.
source: In contrast, neutralizing anti-IL-6Ra antibody (α-IL-6R) inhibited background levels of CD14+ monocytes and CD66b+ granulocytes, as well as Mtb-enhanced myeloid differentiation by CD34+ cell cultures (Figure 4f–h) but not transcription of STAT1 and MX1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data with anti-IL-6R treatment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Megakaryoid, erythroid- or dendritic cell-associated surface molecules were unaltered in α-IL-6R-treated cell cultures.
source: In addition, megakaryoid, erythroid- or dendritic cell-associated surface molecules were unaltered in α-IL-6R-treated cell cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1j–l).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data with anti-IL-6R treatment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1j-l.

claim: Mtb-exposed CD34+ cell cultures treated with α-IL-6R presented significantly lower CFU counts when compared with infected untreated control cell cultures.
source: Interestingly, Mtb-exposed CD34+ cell cultures treated with α-IL-6R (Figure 4i) presented significantly lower CFU counts when compared with infected untreated control cell cultures, while α-IFNAR2 (Figure 4j) or α-IFN-γ (Figure 4k) did not affect CFU counts.
evidence: This is based on CFU data with anti-IL-6R treatment shown in Figure 4i.

claim: α-IFNAR2 or α-IFN-γ did not affect CFU counts in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cell cultures.
source: Interestingly, Mtb-exposed CD34+ cell cultures treated with α-IL-6R (Figure 4i) presented significantly lower CFU counts when compared with infected untreated control cell cultures, while α-IFNAR2 (Figure 4j) or α-IFN-γ (Figure 4k) did not affect CFU counts.
evidence: This is based on CFU data with anti-IFNAR2 and anti-IFN-γ treatment shown in Figure 4j,k.

claim: Live Mtb enhances IL-6R-mediated myeloid differentiation by human CD34+ cells in vitro.
source: Together, these results suggest live Mtb enhances IL-6R-mediated myeloid differentiation by human CD34+ cells in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the antibody neutralization experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: IL6, IL6ST, IL6R and STAT3 were significantly enriched in transcriptomes of active TB monocytes, when compared to cells from healthy controls.
source: As shown in Figure 5a (top panel), IL6, IL6ST, IL6R and STAT3 were significantly enriched in transcriptomes of active TB monocytes, when compared to cells from healthy controls.
evidence: This is based on IPA analysis of published monocyte transcriptome data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: STAT1 and IL1B were confirmed as upstream regulators in active TB monocytes.
source: As reported previously (Berry et al., 2010; Mayer-Barber et al., 2011; Novikov et al., 2011), STAT1 and IL1B were also confirmed as upstream regulators in active TB monocytes (Figure 5a, top panel).
evidence: This is based on IPA analysis shown in Figure 5a and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IRF1 and STAT1 were the only genes in common between the TB monocyte gene signature, the 'IL6/STAT3 pathway' and the 'in vivo IFN-β' signature.
source: Strikingly, the two top upstream regulators in TB monocytes, IRF1 and STAT1 (Figure 5a, top panel), were the only genes in common between the TB monocyte gene signature (Berry et al., 2010), the 'IL6/STAT3 pathway' and the 'in vivo IFN-β" signature (Figure 5a, Venn diagram, bottom panel), suggesting these genes might be regulated by both IL-6 and type I IFN during active TB in vivo.
evidence: This is based on Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5a, bottom panel.

claim: IRF1 and STAT1 might be regulated by both IL-6 and type I IFN during active TB in vivo.
source: Strikingly, the two top upstream regulators in TB monocytes, IRF1 and STAT1 (Figure 5a, top panel), were the only genes in common between the TB monocyte gene signature (Berry et al., 2010), the 'IL6/STAT3 pathway' and the 'in vivo IFN-β" signature (Figure 5a, Venn diagram, bottom panel), suggesting these genes might be regulated by both IL-6 and type I IFN during active TB in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap of gene signatures.

claim: The 'IL6/STAT3' pathway was significantly enriched in the whole blood 'Berry TB' disease signature.
source: In addition to the previously demonstrated type I IFN/STAT1 signature (Berry et al., 2010), the 'IL6/STAT3' pathway was significantly enriched in this data set (FDR-corrected p<10−4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the Berry TB dataset.

claim: STRING network analysis confirmed two clusters comprising 'CD34/myeloid', 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared' pathways.
source: STRING network analysis of protein-protein interactions confirmed two clusters (Figure 5b, bottom panel), which comprised three signatures: 'CD34/myeloid', 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared' pathways.
evidence: This is based on STRING network analysis shown in Figure 5b, bottom panel.

claim: Increased IL-6/STAT3 protein levels and changes in CD34/CD38 homeostasis were found to be early events in TB pathogenesis.
source: Reanalysis of the published 'Scriba Plasma TB' proteome set (Scriba et al., 2017) confirmed increased IL-6/STAT3 protein levels and changes in CD34/CD38 homeostasis, which were found to be early events in TB pathogenesis (Figure 5c, top panel).
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of the Scriba plasma proteome data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: 'IL6/STAT3' pathway-associated proteins increased around 12 months before TB diagnosis.
source: 'IL6/STAT3' pathway-associated proteins such as PLA2G2A, CRP, STAT3, IL-6 and CFB increased around 12 months before TB diagnosis (Figure 5c,d, top panels - orange circles and bars), which was concomitant with significant changes in the 'IFN/IL6-shared' plasma markers CXCL10, IFNAR1 and MMP9 (Figure 5c,d top panels - blue circles and bars).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal analysis of the Scriba plasma proteome data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: Changes in 'IFN/IL6-shared' plasma markers CXCL10, IFNAR1 and MMP9 occurred around 12 months before TB diagnosis.
source: 'IL6/STAT3' pathway-associated proteins such as PLA2G2A, CRP, STAT3, IL-6 and CFB increased around 12 months before TB diagnosis (Figure 5c,d, top panels - orange circles and bars), which was concomitant with significant changes in the 'IFN/IL6-shared' plasma markers CXCL10, IFNAR1 and MMP9 (Figure 5c,d top panels - blue circles and bars).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal analysis of the Scriba plasma proteome data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: The 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared' pathways were significantly enriched in a gene set linked to monocyte expansion in vivo, measured as monocyte:lymphocyte (ML) ratio.
source: The 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared"pathways were also significantly enriched in a gene set recently linked to monocyte expansion in vivo, measured as monocyte:lymphocyte (ML) ratio (Naranbhai et al., 2015) (Supplementary file 2), and positively correlated with mycobacterial growth in vitro, thus connecting monocyte expansion and increased Mtb survival.
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis of the ML ratio gene set.

claim: The 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared' pathways positively correlated with mycobacterial growth in vitro.
source: The 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared"pathways were also significantly enriched in a gene set recently linked to monocyte expansion in vivo, measured as monocyte:lymphocyte (ML) ratio (Naranbhai et al., 2015) (Supplementary file 2), and positively correlated with mycobacterial growth in vitro, thus connecting monocyte expansion and increased Mtb survival.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis connecting gene expression with CFU data.

claim: Changes in the 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared' pathways preceded enrichment of the 'ML ratio' gene set during development of TB disease.
source: Interestingly, the changes found in both the 'IL6/STAT3' and 'IFN/IL6-shared' pathways during development of TB disease preceded enrichment of the 'ML ratio' gene set (Naranbhai et al., 2015) (6 months before diagnosis, p<0.05, Figure 5c, bottom panel and Figure 5d, top panel, gray bar) and reduction of the CD34/CD38 gene markers, in agreement with our in vitro model of Mtb-enhanced CD34+ differentiation (CD34+ → CD34+CD38+ → CD14+).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of the Scriba plasma proteome data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: CD34+ cells exposed to Mtb in vitro displayed increased levels of pSTAT1 as well as C/EBPβ (and a slight enhancement of C/EBPα).
source: In support of this idea, CD34+ cells exposed to Mtb in vitro displayed increased levels of pSTAT1 as well as C/EBPβ (and a slight enhancement of C/EBPα), which are key TF regulators of ISGs and myeloid differentiation genes, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: pSTAT1 and C/EBPβ are key TF regulators of ISGs and myeloid differentiation genes, respectively.
source: In support of this idea, CD34+ cells exposed to Mtb in vitro displayed increased levels of pSTAT1 as well as C/EBPβ (and a slight enhancement of C/EBPα), which are key TF regulators of ISGs and myeloid differentiation genes, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these transcription factors.

claim: qPCR experiments from HK Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells did not show induction of myeloid differentiation TFs CEBPA and CEBPB.
source: Interestingly, qPCR experiments from HK Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells did not show induction of myeloid differentiation TFs CEBPA and CEBPB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g.

claim: CEBPB, CEBPD and STAT3 as well as IRF1, STAT1 and ICSBP/IRF8 TFs were significantly enriched in Mtb-infected CD34+ transcriptomes.
source: Furthermore, we observed that CEBPB, CEBPD and STAT3 as well as IRF1, STAT1 and ICSBP/IRF8 TFs were significantly enriched in Mtb-infected CD34+ transcriptomes (Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b - Figure 2—source data 1), which were associated with increased mycobacterial replication in vitro (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is based on transcription factor enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Enrichment of CEBPB, CEBPD, STAT3, IRF1, STAT1 and ICSBP/IRF8 TFs in Mtb-infected CD34+ transcriptomes was associated with increased mycobacterial replication in vitro.
source: Furthermore, we observed that CEBPB, CEBPD and STAT3 as well as IRF1, STAT1 and ICSBP/IRF8 TFs were significantly enriched in Mtb-infected CD34+ transcriptomes (Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b - Figure 2—source data 1), which were associated with increased mycobacterial replication in vitro (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is an inference connecting transcription factor enrichment with CFU data.

claim: Mtb infection activates a gene module shared by both type I IFN and IL-6, linking downstream ISGs and CEBPs.
source: These results suggest that Mtb infection activates a gene module shared by both type I IFN and IL-6, linking downstream ISGs and CEBPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcriptomic and systems biology analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Both the monocyte counts and ML ratio were significantly increased in active TB patients when compared to latent TB subjects.
source: When compared to latent TB subjects, we observed that both the monocyte counts and ML ratio were significantly increased in active TB patients (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of the Berry et al., 2010 dataset shown in Figure 5f.

claim: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with ML ratio levels.
source: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with ML ratio levels (Figure 5g), IL6R transcripts (Figure 5h), STAT3 (Figure 5i) as well as inflammatory biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the Berry et al., 2010 dataset shown in Figure 5g.

claim: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with IL6R transcripts.
source: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with ML ratio levels (Figure 5g), IL6R transcripts (Figure 5h), STAT3 (Figure 5i) as well as inflammatory biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the Berry et al., 2010 dataset shown in Figure 5h.

claim: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with STAT3.
source: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with ML ratio levels (Figure 5g), IL6R transcripts (Figure 5h), STAT3 (Figure 5i) as well as inflammatory biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the Berry et al., 2010 dataset shown in Figure 5i.

claim: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with inflammatory biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).
source: CEBPB transcripts positively correlated with ML ratio levels (Figure 5g), IL6R transcripts (Figure 5h), STAT3 (Figure 5i) as well as inflammatory biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: CEBPB mRNA levels were significantly higher in Mtb-positive vs. Mtb-negative sputum smears.
source: In addition, CEBPB mRNA levels were significantly higher in Mtb-positive vs. Mtb-negative sputum smears (Figure 5j), and positively correlated to tissue damage, total symptom counts as well as ISG15 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), in agreement with our previous findings (Dos Santos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Berry et al., 2010 dataset shown in Figure 5j.

claim: CEBPB mRNA levels positively correlated to tissue damage, total symptom counts as well as ISG15 levels.
source: In addition, CEBPB mRNA levels were significantly higher in Mtb-positive vs. Mtb-negative sputum smears (Figure 5j), and positively correlated to tissue damage, total symptom counts as well as ISG15 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), in agreement with our previous findings (Dos Santos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The IL6/IL6R/CEBP gene module is a hub correlated with monocyte expansion during Mtb infection in vivo and is amplified in severe pulmonary and systemic disease.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the IL6/IL6R/CEBP gene module is a hub correlated with monocyte expansion during Mtb infection in vivo and is amplified in severe pulmonary and systemic disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integrated systems biology analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: ISGs have been undergoing strong purifying selection during primate evolution.
source: It has been reported that these ISGs have been undergoing strong purifying selection during primate evolution (Manry et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2017), including recent Neanderthal introgression (Enard and Petrov, 2018; Quach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Manry et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2017; Enard and Petrov, 2018; Quach et al., 2016.

claim: ISGs have undergone recent Neanderthal introgression.
source: It has been reported that these ISGs have been undergoing strong purifying selection during primate evolution (Manry et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2017), including recent Neanderthal introgression (Enard and Petrov, 2018; Quach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Enard and Petrov, 2018; Quach et al., 2016.

claim: IL-6, IL-6R and C/EBP family members C/EBPα, C/EBPβ and C/EBPδ differ substantially throughout primate evolution and even among closely related hominins.
source: STRING network measurements of amino acid conservation and gene co-occurrence across mammalian and primate evolution revealed that IL-6, IL-6R and C/EBP family members C/EBPα, C/EBPβ and C/EBPδ differ substantially throughout primate evolution and even among closely related hominins (Pan troglodytes and Gorilla gorilla) (Figure 6a, heat map).
evidence: This is based on STRING network conservation analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: KLF5/NFKB1/MAPK1//STAT1/STAT3 remained largely conserved in most mammals, and even in birds and reptiles.
source: In contrast, matched control molecules in the same STRING network (KLF5/NFKB1/MAPK1//STAT1/STAT3) remained largely conserved in most mammals, and even in birds and reptiles (Figure 6a, heat map and Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is based on STRING network conservation analysis shown in Figure 6a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The conserved 'IFN/IL6-shared' genes CXCL10/CXCL9/STAT1/STAT2 displayed higher fold-changes upon type I IFN treatment across all 10 species (from chicken to human).
source: As expected, the conserved 'IFN/IL6-shared' genes CXCL10/CXCL9/STAT1/STAT2 displayed higher fold-changes upon type I IFN treatment across all 10 species (from chicken to human, Figure 6b, top panel).
evidence: This is based on cross-species type I IFN regulation analysis shown in Figure 6b, top panel.

claim: The 'IL-6/STAT3' pathway genes IL6, STAT3 and SOCS3 were significantly upregulated upon type I IFN treatment across species.
source: Interestingly, the 'IL-6/STAT3' pathway genes IL6, STAT3 and SOCS3 were also significantly upregulated while IL6R was significantly down-regulated (Figure 6b, top panel) in the same experimental setting.
evidence: This is based on cross-species type I IFN regulation analysis shown in Figure 6b, top panel.

claim: IL6R was significantly down-regulated upon type I IFN treatment across species.
source: Interestingly, the 'IL-6/STAT3' pathway genes IL6, STAT3 and SOCS3 were also significantly upregulated while IL6R was significantly down-regulated (Figure 6b, top panel) in the same experimental setting.
evidence: This is based on cross-species type I IFN regulation analysis shown in Figure 6b, top panel.

claim: ICSBP/IRF8 and CD38 were strongly upregulated by type I IFN, but only in 4/10 and 2/10 species, respectively.
source: Among CD34/myeloid differentiation genes, ICSBP/IRF8 and CD38 were strongly upregulated, but only in 4/10 and 2/10 species, respectively, while ELF1 was homogeneously and significantly upregulated in 9/10 species (Figure 6b, top panel).
evidence: This is based on cross-species type I IFN regulation analysis shown in Figure 6b, top panel.

claim: ELF1 was homogeneously and significantly upregulated in 9/10 species upon type I IFN treatment.
source: Among CD34/myeloid differentiation genes, ICSBP/IRF8 and CD38 were strongly upregulated, but only in 4/10 and 2/10 species, respectively, while ELF1 was homogeneously and significantly upregulated in 9/10 species (Figure 6b, top panel).
evidence: This is based on cross-species type I IFN regulation analysis shown in Figure 6b, top panel.

claim: Type I IFN consistently regulates expression of IL-6 signaling and myeloid-associated genes in different species.
source: These results suggest that type I IFN consistently regulates expression of IL-6 signaling and myeloid-associated genes in different species.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cross-species analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: CEBPB was the topmost variable ISG across mammalian evolution.
source: However, among the entire IL6/IL6R/CEBP myeloid gene set, CEBPB was the topmost variable ISG across mammalian evolution (CV >1000%, Figure 6b, bottom panel).
evidence: This is based on coefficient of variation analysis shown in Figure 6b, bottom panel.

claim: Type I IFN-induced upregulation of both CEBPB and CEBPD was present only in humans and lacking in all other mammals investigated.
source: Remarkably, type I IFN-induced upregulation of both CEBPB and CEBPD, previously identified as NF-IL6 and NF-IL6β, respectively (Ramji and Foka, 2002) was present only in humans and lacking in all other mammals investigated (Figure 6b, bottom panel, inset).
evidence: This is based on cross-species type I IFN regulation analysis shown in Figure 6b, bottom panel, inset.

claim: ChipSeq analysis confirmed the existence of functional STAT1 peaks in CEBPB and CEBPD in IFN-treated human CD14+ monocytes.
source: Mechanistically, ChipSeq analysis of IFN-treated human CD14+ monocytes corresponding to regions with active chromatin (DNase Hypersensitivity Sites, DHS and H3K27 acetylation, not shown) confirmed the existence of functional STAT1 peaks in CEBPB and CEBPD (Figure 6c, top and middle panels, denoted by vertical blue lines).
evidence: This is based on ChipSeq analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: STAT1 peaks in CEBPB and CEBPD correlated with increased downstream transcription in CD14+ cells, as compared to purified CD34+ cells.
source: These peaks correlated with increased downstream transcription in CD14+ cells, as compared to purified CD34+ cells (Figure 6c, RNA-seq).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Only 3 out of 11 (27%) STAT1 binding peaks in CEBPB and CEBPD were found in conserved regions.
source: In agreement with our findings (represented in Figure 6b, bottom panel, inset), only 3 out of 11 (27%) STAT1 binding peaks in CEBPB and CEBPD were found in conserved regions (Conservation Birds-Mammals line, Figure 6c), while 6 out of 7 (86%) STAT1 peaks were conserved in CXCL9 and CXCL10 genes (Figure 6c, bottom panel).
evidence: This is based on conservation analysis of ChipSeq peaks shown in Figure 6c.

claim: 6 out of 7 (86%) STAT1 peaks were conserved in CXCL9 and CXCL10 genes.
source: In agreement with our findings (represented in Figure 6b, bottom panel, inset), only 3 out of 11 (27%) STAT1 binding peaks in CEBPB and CEBPD were found in conserved regions (Conservation Birds-Mammals line, Figure 6c), while 6 out of 7 (86%) STAT1 peaks were conserved in CXCL9 and CXCL10 genes (Figure 6c, bottom panel).
evidence: This is based on conservation analysis of ChipSeq peaks shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Transcriptional regulation of CEBPB and CEBPD in humans and macaques, but not mouse cells stimulated with double-stranded RNA, was observed.
source: Interestingly, transcriptional regulation of CEBPB and CEBPD in humans and macaques, but not mouse cells stimulated with double-stranded RNA, which mimics a viral infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), were also observed in an independent data set (Hagai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of an independent dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: CXCL9 and CXCL10 responses are conserved in dsRNA-stimulated cells from humans, macaques and mouse.
source: As expected, CXCL9 and CXCL10 responses are conserved in dsRNA-stimulated cells from humans, macaques and mouse (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of an independent dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Transcriptional induction of CEBPB and CEBPD controlled by IL-6- and type I IFN-signaling appears as a relatively recent event in mammalian and primate evolution.
source: Thus, transcriptional induction of CEBPB and CEBPD controlled by IL-6- and type I IFN-signaling appears as a relatively recent event in mammalian and primate evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evolutionary analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Eleven genes with Neanderthal introgression were significantly upregulated in Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells transcriptome.
source: As shown in Figure 6d (Figure 2—source data 1), eleven genes with Neanderthal introgression were significantly upregulated in our Mtb-exposed CD34+ cells transcriptome (enrichment p<0.0001).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis of Neanderthal introgression genes and Mtb-exposed CD34+ DEGs shown in Figure 6d.

claim: OAS1, OAS2 and MT2A transcripts had significantly higher effect sizes upon ML ratios, as compared to other introgressed genes.
source: Of those, OAS1, OAS2 and MT2A transcripts had significantly higher effect sizes upon ML ratios, as compared to other introgressed genes (p<0.05) and to all other genes shown to regulate ML ratio in vivo (p<0.001, Figure 6d).
evidence: This is based on effect size analysis shown in Figure 6d, bottom left panel.

claim: 9 out of 11 introgressed genes enriched during Mtb-triggered monocyte differentiation were significantly upregulated in TLR1/TLR2-stimulated monocytes from individuals of European descendance.
source: Strikingly, 9 out of 11 introgressed genes enriched during Mtb-triggered monocyte differentiation (Figure 6d, Venn diagram) were significantly upregulated in TLR1/TLR2-stimulated (Figure 6d, right panel), but not unstimulated monocytes (not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Quach et al., 2016 dataset shown in Figure 6d, right panel.

claim: Pathogen exposure may enhance gene pathways recently selected during hominid evolution linked to monocyte expansion.
source: These findings suggest pathogen exposure may enhance gene pathways recently selected during hominid evolution linked to monocyte expansion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Neanderthal introgression and monocyte stimulation data.

claim: Two large GWAS studies containing >230,000 individuals have identified single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in or adjacent to IL6R, CEBPA-CEBPD-CEBPE and ICSBP/IRF8 genes as significantly associated to blood monocyte counts.
source: Two large GWAS studies (Astle et al., 2016; Kanai et al., 2018) containing >230,000 individuals have identified single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in or adjacent to IL6R, CEBPA-CEBPD-CEBPE and ICSBP/IRF8 genes as significantly associated to blood monocyte counts (Supplementary file 2 and ranked in Figure 7a as monocyte count GWAS).
evidence: This is based on GWAS data from Astle et al., 2016 and Kanai et al., 2018.

claim: Gene-specific z-scores for human polygenic adaptation to pathogens were positive for all genes in the IL6/IL6R/CEBP myeloid differentiation module (except CXCL10).
source: Moreover, gene-specific z-scores for human polygenic adaptation to pathogens in 51 different populations worldwide (Daub et al., 2013) were positive, representing higher levels of population differentiation, for all genes in our proposed IL6/IL6R/CEBP myeloid differentiation module (except CXCL10, Figure 7a and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on pathogen adaptation z-scores from Daub et al., 2013 shown in Figure 7a.

claim: A significant enrichment for differentially expressed genes from Mtb-exposed CD34+ transcriptome and TB susceptibility GWAS/candidate genes was observed.
source: A significant enrichment (p<0.0001) for differentially expressed genes from our Mtb-exposed CD34+ transcriptome and TB susceptibility GWAS/candidate genes (18 out of 172 genes, including IL6, STAT1 and CD14) was also observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A significant overlap was found for the IL6/IL6R/CEPB module and TB genetic susceptibility (six shared genes CD14, CXCL10, IL6, IL6R, IRF1 and STAT1).
source: Similarly, a significant (p<0.0001) overlap was found for the IL6/IL6R/CEPB module and TB genetic susceptibility (six shared genes CD14, CXCL10, IL6, IL6R, IRF1 and STAT1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: 24 out of 28 members of the IL6/IL6R/CEBP gene module display a genome-wide, transcriptomic, proteomic or functional association to human TB.
source: As ranked in Figure 7a, 24 out of 28 members of this gene module display a genome-wide, transcriptomic, proteomic or functional association to human TB, being strongest for IL6 and its downstream signaling TFs CEBPB and CEBPD, demonstrated in 5–6 independent data sets each.
evidence: This is based on the integrated ranking shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The association to human TB is strongest for IL6 and its downstream signaling TFs CEBPB and CEBPD, demonstrated in 5–6 independent data sets each.
source: As ranked in Figure 7a, 24 out of 28 members of this gene module display a genome-wide, transcriptomic, proteomic or functional association to human TB, being strongest for IL6 and its downstream signaling TFs CEBPB and CEBPD, demonstrated in 5–6 independent data sets each.
evidence: This is based on the integrated ranking shown in Figure 7a.
